opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the $100 million number that gets thrown around is basically a rental-cost framing. It's roughly: take the number of GPU-hours you needed for the final training run, multiply by what you'd pay per hour to rent those GPUs, and you get something on the order of $100 million. And that's a reasonable way to think about the marginal cost of that one run. But it really understates what it takes to actually *have* that cluster.

If you think about it from the perspective of building the thing, GPT-4 was reportedly trained on something like 25,000 A100s. An A100 at the time was, call it, $10,000 to $15,000 a chip, but that's just the chip. You need the servers, the networking (the InfiniBand fabric is a big chunk), the storage, the datacenter itself, the power and cooling infrastructure. When you add all of that up, the capex for a cluster of that scale is more like a few hundred million dollars, maybe half a billion. The rental number is essentially amortizing that over the useful life of the hardware, and it assumes someone else ate the upfront investment.

And then there's everything that isn't the final run. You don't just do one training run. You do tons of experiments, ablations, smaller-scale runs to figure out your scaling laws, failed runs, restarts. The compute you spend on research and de-risking is plausibly comparable to or larger than the final run itself. So if you're asking "what did it cost to produce GPT-4," the final-run rental price is kind of the tip of the iceberg.

The reason this matters is when you start extrapolating. If you think the trend is roughly half an order of magnitude of compute per year, and you anchor on the true cluster cost rather than the rental figure, you get to multi-billion-dollar clusters very quickly, then tens of billions, and by the end of the decade you're plausibly talking about hundred-billion-dollar or even trillion-dollar clusters. That's a very different picture from "oh, it's a hundred million bucks, any mid-size company can do that." The real numbers point to this becoming an industrial mobilization, measured in gigawatts of power and a meaningful fraction of national electricity production, and that's what I think people are underrating.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the roughly $100 million GPU-hour rental estimate for the final run with the much larger capital cost of building and equipping the cluster.

r002.rationale: It says the rental estimate assumes someone else paid the upfront investment, but does not state that the largest cluster cannot simply be rented for the few months needed.

fable-5.1.text:
So the $100 million number people throw around is, I think, roughly the compute cost of the actual training run. It's like, you take the number of GPU-hours, you multiply by some cloud rental rate, and you get something in that ballpark. And that's a fine number for what it is. But it's really not the number you care about if you're asking "what did it cost to be in a position to train GPT-4?"

Because what actually happens is you have to build the cluster. You have to buy the GPUs, you have to buy the networking, you have to find the datacenter, the power, the cooling. And a cluster that can train GPT-4 in a few months is tens of thousands of A100s. That's billions of dollars of capex, not a hundred million. The training run is a few months of utilization on an asset that cost you way more than that to stand up. If you amortize correctly, sure, you get some fraction of the capex, but the point is somebody had to write the check for the whole thing up front, and they wrote it in advance of knowing the model would work.

And then on top of that there's everything that isn't the final run. There's all the experiments, all the scaling-law runs, all the stuff that didn't work, the ablations, the smaller models you train to de-risk the big one. In practice a huge fraction of your compute goes to research, not to the one headline run. And the people. You've got hundreds of very expensive researchers and engineers working on this for a year or two, and the infrastructure engineering to actually make a 25,000-GPU job run without falling over every few hours is enormously hard and enormously expensive.

So when I think about it, I think of the training run cost as the marginal cost of the last step, and the real question is the total cost of the program, which is the cluster plus the research compute plus the talent. And once you look at it that way, you're already in the billions for the GPT-4 generation. Which matters, because the extrapolation is the interesting part. If you think of this as "oh, a hundred million, that's a rounding error for a big tech company," you miss that the next generation is a ten-billion-dollar cluster, and the one after that is a hundred billion, and then you're talking about trillion-dollar clusters and like gigawatts and tens of gigawatts of power. The capex trajectory is the story, and the hundred-million framing obscures how steep it actually is.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes the roughly $100 million compute cost calculated using GPU-hours and rental rates from the much larger cost of buying and standing up the cluster.

r002.rationale: It says the cluster must be built and that the training run uses the resulting asset for a few months, but does not state that a cluster of this scale cannot simply be rented for those months.

You’re using the GPUs for a few months, and you’re charging some fraction of their useful life to that run. But to actually build that cluster, you have to buy all the GPUs upfront, plus the networking and the rest of the infrastructure. So you can have a training run that costs $100 million on an underlying cluster that costs a billion dollars. And that’s before you account for the experiments and failed runs that went into getting the final run right.

The GPUs have a useful life of several years, and then you also need networking, servers, power, cooling, and the rest of the data center infrastructure. So the cluster itself could cost substantially more than $100 million, even if that’s the compute cost you assign to one training run.
